title: Consensus & Leader Election
subtitle: How machines that can't trust the network agree on one answer
objectives: Explain why agreement is hard when messages can be lost, delayed, or duplicated
Describe how majority quorums make split-brain impossible rather than unlikely
Walk through leader election, terms, and why a fencing token is required
Decide when you need consensus — and why the answer is usually 'use the thing that already has it'

exercises.prompt: Five servers must agree on one value: who is the leader. Why can't they just vote and be done?
choices: Messages can be lost, delayed, or arrive out of order — so a node that hears nothing can't tell whether a vote was never sent, or sent and lost, or is still in flight
exercises.why: Voting is trivial when everyone reliably hears everyone; the difficulty is that the network gives you no such promise, and silence is ambiguous. A node observing nothing cannot distinguish a dead peer from a slow one from a lost message — which is unit 10's 'dead or just slow?' being the fundamental obstacle rather than an annoyance.

exercises.prompt: Why does 'just add a timeout' not solve it?
choices: A timeout converts 'I don't know' into a guess: too short and you declare a healthy node dead, too long and you stay stuck — the uncertainty doesn't go away, you just pick which way to be wrong
exercises.why: A timeout is a decision procedure for an undecidable question, so it doesn't remove the ambiguity — it converts it into a configurable error. This is the same shape as the failover timeout from unit 10 and the health check interval from unit 12, which is the point: these aren't three problems, they're one problem you keep meeting.

exercises.prompt: ______ is the problem of getting multiple machines to agree on a single value despite failures.
exercises.why: One value, many machines, an unreliable network — and everyone must end up believing the same thing, or the disagreement becomes corruption.

exercises.prompt: What goes wrong if two nodes both believe they're the leader?
choices: Nothing — more leaders means more capacity
Both accept writes, producing two divergent histories with no principled way to merge them — split brain
exercises.why: This is unit 10's split brain, and it's the failure consensus exists to prevent: two authorities means two truths, and truths that diverged independently can't be reconciled by any rule you invent afterwards. Note it's worse than an outage — an outage stops and recovers, whereas divergence silently corrupts and you find out later.

exercises.prompt: What must a consensus algorithm guarantee? Select all.
choices: Agreement — no two nodes decide different values
Validity — the decided value was actually proposed by someone
Termination — it eventually decides, provided enough nodes are up and can communicate
That it always decides quickly, no matter what
exercises.why: Agreement, validity, and eventual termination are what these algorithms actually promise. Speed is not on the list, and can't be: the FLP result says that with even one possible failure and no timing assumptions, no algorithm can guarantee it always terminates — which is why real systems lean on timeouts and accept 'usually fast, occasionally stalls' as the honest deal.

exercises.prompt: So why is 'agreement' the property worth paying for?
choices: Because disagreement isn't a delay — it's divergent state that no later process can repair, so preventing it is worth waiting for
exercises.why: A stalled decision costs you time and resolves; a wrong decision costs you your data's integrity and doesn't. That asymmetry justifies the entire expense of consensus — you're buying the impossibility of a failure that has no cleanup, using a currency (latency) that you can recover from.

exercises.prompt: 5 nodes. A rule says a decision needs 3 votes. A partition splits them 3 and 2. Why can't both sides decide?
choices: Only one side can hold 3 of 5 — two disjoint groups cannot both contain a majority, so at most one side can ever proceed
The rule is enforced by a coordinator
exercises.why: It's arithmetic doing the safety work: two groups that don't overlap can't both have more than half, so the majority rule makes two simultaneous leaders impossible rather than unlikely. That's the crucial word — impossible. The 2-node side isn't trusted to behave; it's mathematically unable to gather the votes.

exercises.prompt: Why do consensus clusters use odd numbers of nodes — 3, 5, 7?
choices: 4 nodes need 3 for a majority, exactly like 3 nodes do — so the 4th node adds cost and tolerates no additional failure
Even numbers can't form a majority
exercises.why: Majority of 3 is 2, so 3 nodes survive 1 failure; majority of 4 is 3, so 4 nodes also survive only 1. You paid for another machine and bought exactly nothing in fault tolerance — and gave yourself one more thing that can break. Going 3 → 5 is what buys the second failure, which is why cluster sizes step by twos.

exercises.prompt: A consensus cluster has 7 nodes. How many can fail while the cluster still makes progress?
exercises.why: Majority of 7 is 4, so as long as 4 remain you have a quorum — meaning 3 can fail. The general rule is that 2f+1 nodes tolerate f failures, which is why 3 tolerates 1 and 5 tolerates 2.

exercises.prompt: Why does a majority quorum guarantee the new leader has all committed writes?
choices: A write is only committed once a majority stored it, and any new leader must be elected by a majority — those two majorities must overlap, so someone in the electing group has the write
The old leader hands over its log
exercises.why: It's the same pigeonhole argument as unit 19's W+R>N: two majorities of the same set always share at least one member, so the electing quorum necessarily contains a node that saw every committed write. That's why committed data survives a leader dying — not because anyone hands it over, but because it was impossible for a majority to have missed it.

exercises.prompt: Your 5-node cluster is split into 2 and 2 and 1 by a network fault. What happens?
choices: Nobody has a majority, so the cluster makes no progress at all — it stays consistent by being entirely unavailable
exercises.why: No group of 2 or 1 can reach 3, so nobody can be elected and nothing can be committed — the cluster is fully down while every node is perfectly healthy. That is CP behaving exactly as designed: it chose consistency, and this is what choosing consistency costs on a bad day. A system that stayed up here would be a system willing to fork its own history.

exercises.prompt: Is a majority quorum protecting you from nodes that lie or send corrupted messages?
choices: No — algorithms like Raft assume nodes may crash or be unreachable, but not that they actively lie; surviving liars is Byzantine fault tolerance, which is far more expensive
Yes, if you use enough nodes
exercises.why: The failure model matters as much as the algorithm: Raft and Paxos handle crash-stop faults, where a node either works correctly or stops, and that assumption is what makes them affordable. Tolerating malicious or arbitrarily buggy nodes needs Byzantine protocols with more nodes and more rounds — which is why they show up in blockchains, where participants genuinely aren't trusted, and almost never inside your own datacenter.

exercises.prompt: Why elect a single leader at all, if consensus can decide any value?
choices: Because running full consensus for every operation is expensive — elect once, and then one node can sequence writes cheaply until it fails
exercises.why: Consensus is the expensive part, so you spend it rarely — on 'who decides?' — and then the leader orders operations by itself, turning per-write agreement into per-write replication. This is unit 10's single-leader design earning its keep: one writer removes conflicts by construction, and now you know how the leader gets chosen safely.

exercises.prompt: Order a Raft-style leader election.
steps: Followers hear nothing from the leader for a timeout
One follower becomes a candidate and increments the term
It requests votes from every other node
Nodes grant a vote if they haven't already voted in that term
With a majority, the candidate becomes leader and starts sending heartbeats
exercises.why: Silence starts it, a term number labels the attempt, and a majority ends it. The heartbeat is what keeps the peace: as long as followers hear from the leader they never start an election, so the leader's continued existence is asserted continuously rather than assumed.

exercises.prompt: What is the 'term' number actually doing?
choices: Counting how long the leader has served
Acting as a logical clock: each election gets a higher term, so any message from an older term is recognisably stale and rejected
exercises.why: Terms give you an ordering of leadership epochs without needing a wall clock anyone agrees on — the exact problem unit 19 flagged with last-write-wins. A deposed leader that wakes up still believing it's in charge is carrying an old term number, so every node it contacts can tell instantly that it's behind and refuse it.

exercises.prompt: Two candidates start elections simultaneously and split the vote — nobody gets a majority. What stops this repeating forever?
choices: Randomized election timeouts — each node waits a different random interval, so one almost always starts first next round and wins uncontested
exercises.why: Identical timeouts make nodes act in unison, which is exactly what causes repeated split votes — the same synchronization trap as unit 17's clients all obeying one `Retry-After`. Randomizing breaks the symmetry cheaply: someone times out first, requests votes while everyone else is still waiting, and the round resolves.

exercises.prompt: A leader is deposed while paused, but doesn't know it. It wakes up and writes to shared storage. How do you stop it corrupting data?
choices: Fencing tokens: every leader gets a monotonically increasing number, storage remembers the highest it has seen, and a write carrying an older token is rejected
exercises.why: You can't prevent a paused leader from waking up and acting, so the protection must live at the resource rather than rely on the leader behaving. Fencing makes the storage itself the arbiter: it has seen token 6, so a write stamped 5 is provably from a deposed leader and gets refused. This is unit 10's fencing made concrete — and note the resource must participate, since a lock service alone cannot stop a client that's stopped listening.

exercises.prompt: During an election, what happens to writes?
choices: They stop — there's no leader to sequence them, so the system is unavailable for writes until one is elected
They queue on the old leader
exercises.why: No leader means nobody may order writes, so an election is a small planned outage measured in the election timeout — typically hundreds of milliseconds to seconds. That's the price of single-leader safety, and it's why timeout tuning is a real tradeoff: shorter means faster recovery and more spurious elections during blips, longer means fewer false alarms and a longer write outage when a leader genuinely dies.

exercises.prompt: Your team proposes implementing Raft in-house for a service that needs leader election. Reaction?
choices: Don't: consensus is notoriously hard to get right, and the failure mode is silent corruption discovered later. Use etcd, ZooKeeper, or your database's built-in election
exercises.why: Raft is understandable to read and brutal to implement correctly, because the bugs live in rare interleavings — a node pausing at exactly the wrong moment, a message arriving after you assumed it couldn't. Those don't show up in tests; they show up as divergent data in production months later. Mature implementations have absorbed years of exactly those, which is what you're actually buying.

exercises.prompt: Which genuinely need consensus? Select all.
choices: Deciding which database replica is the leader
Distributed locks that must never be held twice
exercises.why: Leadership, locks, and membership share one property: two different answers is a catastrophe, so paying for agreement is worth it. Page views are the opposite — a count that's briefly off by three costs nothing, so coordinating every increment would buy a guarantee nobody needed. The test is simply whether disagreement corrupts something or merely annoys someone.

exercises.prompt: Why is running consensus across regions usually a bad idea?
choices: Every decision needs a majority to reply, so a cross-region quorum means every write waits on a round trip of ~100ms or more — the speed of light becomes your write latency
exercises.why: Consensus is round trips, and a round trip across the planet is unit 4's physics rather than a tuning problem — a cross-continent quorum makes every write cost hundreds of milliseconds, forever. That's why most systems keep the consensus group inside one region and replicate asynchronously across them, accepting the failure modes of unit 10 in exchange for writes that don't wait on an ocean.

exercises.prompt: You need a distributed lock so only one worker runs a nightly job. Slide toward your approach.
exercises.rightLabel: A row in your existing database
exercises.why: For one nightly job, a conditional insert or update in the database you already run gives you mutual exclusion with a component you already operate — and if two workers ever both ran, you'd rerun a job rather than lose money. Reach for a dedicated consensus service when the lock protects something where double-execution is genuinely unacceptable, and you're willing to run and understand another distributed system to get it.

exercises.prompt: You use a lock service, and it says you hold the lock. Is it safe to write?
choices: Yes — that's what the lock means
Not by itself: you might be paused and the lease expired without you noticing, so safety needs a fencing token the storage checks — the lock alone can't stop a client that's stopped listening
Yes, if the lock is fresh
Only if the lock service is CP
exercises.why: A lock is a lease, and a lease expires on the service's clock rather than yours — so a long garbage-collection pause can leave you holding an expired lock while feeling certain. This is the famous gap: correctness has to be enforced where the write lands, via a fencing token, because no amount of asking the lock service can tell you whether you were frozen since you last asked.

exercises.prompt: What's the honest summary of consensus?
choices: It's how distributed systems stay fast

It's the expensive machinery that makes disagreement impossible rather than unlikely — so use it for the few decisions where two answers is a catastrophe, run it inside one region, and don't implement it yourself
It removes the need for replication
exercises.why: Consensus buys you the one thing nothing else can — a decision that cannot fork — and charges round trips and unavailability when a majority is unreachable. Everything in this unit followed from the same fact you met in unit 10 and again in 18: you cannot tell dead from slow, so agreement must be constructed from majorities rather than assumed from silence.
